subject: Cognitive Science
title: Naive Theories
description: Learn Naive Theories in one minute.

hook.text: Ask a child why it's cold in winter. She'll say the sun is farther away. It's logical—and completely wrong.

buildup.text: Naive theories are intuitive models we build from everyday experience before formal education.

discovery.text: They're surprisingly stable. Even physics students revert to naive theories under time pressure.

twist.text: Naive theories aren't random—they follow consistent internal logic, which is why they're hard to replace.

climax.text: Good teaching doesn't just add facts—it confronts and restructures existing mental models.

punchline.text: What feels obvious is often wrong.

quiz.question: Why are naive theories hard to correct?

details.summary: Naive theories are intuitive explanations people naturally develop about how the world works without formal education. Children and adults hold naive theories about physics, biology, and psychology that are often wrong but systematic and deeply held.
details.whyItMatters: Naive theories explain why misconceptions persist even after education. You cannot teach effectively without understanding the wrong theory a student already holds.
takeaways: People develop intuitive theories without formal instruction
Naive theories are systematic, not random misconceptions
Effective teaching must address existing naive theories directly

faq.question: What is a common naive theory in physics?
faq.answer: Many people believe a moving object needs continuous force to keep moving, the impetus theory. This contradicts Newton's first law but matches everyday experience where friction eventually stops things. Even after physics courses, students often revert to this intuition under pressure.

faq.question: Why are naive theories so hard to change?
faq.answer: Because they work well enough in daily life. Your intuitive physics gets you through most situations. Naive theories are reinforced by years of experience. Changing them requires not just new information but restructuring an entire framework of understanding, which is cognitively costly.
